title: Design ETA prediction and courier capacity planning for a food-delivery app
prompt:
**Interviewer:** A food-delivery app runs in **40 cities** and handles **1.2 million orders per day**; the evening peak is about **3 times** the afternoon level. Today the app shows a fixed ETA per restaurant. **22%** of orders arrive more than 10 minutes later than promised, and support tickets about lateness are the top complaint. Couriers are scheduled one week ahead in shifts; recruiting and onboarding a new courier takes about **3 weeks**.

Design (1) an **ETA prediction** system that shows a promised delivery window, and (2) a **courier capacity forecast** for weekly shift planning. Discuss data, models, evaluation, serving and what can go wrong.

sections.label: Requirements & decision
sections.hint: Who uses ETA (customer, dispatch)? What do late and early cost? Capacity horizon vs lead time?

sections.label: Data & features
sections.hint: Order events, GPS, restaurant prep, traffic, weather, supply. Point-in-time. Label definition.

sections.label: Models & baselines
sections.hint: Baseline, GBM regression vs quantile, uncertainty, capacity model (orders per zone-hour).

sections.label: Evaluation & backtest
sections.hint: MAE, P90, bias, coverage, on-time rate, segments; offline vs online experiments.

sections.label: Serving & scale
sections.hint: Latency budget, QPS, feature store online path, batch for capacity, fallbacks.

sections.label: Monitoring & failure modes
sections.hint: Drift, outages, weather shocks, feedback loops, incentives, ETA gaming.

model_answer.req:
**Two products.** (1) ETA: shown to the customer at checkout and used by dispatch. Decision: promise a window so that most orders arrive inside it, without scaring customers with an overly long number. (2) Capacity: weekly shift planning of couriers per city-zone-hour.

**Costs.** Late delivery: complaints, refunds, churn. Too long a promise: lower conversion at checkout. Choose a promised quantile around **P80-P85** and a window like 'P20-P80'; tune from an A/B test on conversion versus late-rate and support tickets. Current baseline: 22% late by more than 10 minutes.

**Capacity.** Forecast **orders per zone per hour** one to four weeks ahead, convert to couriers using productivity (orders per courier-hour), add headroom for the upper quantile. Lead time for recruiting is 3 weeks, so a longer-range forecast (4-8 weeks) of weekly volume is needed for hiring; the weekly shift plan needs the next 7-14 days.

**Success.** ETA: on-time rate (arrive before the promised upper bound) of at least 85%, lower MAE and P90 error, and no loss of conversion. Capacity: fewer unfilled peak hours and lower idle courier hours.
model_answer.data:
**Events.** Order placed, accepted by restaurant, food ready, courier assigned, pickup, drop-off. Label = actual delivery duration (placed to delivered) and also its components (prep, wait for courier, travel).

**Features at order time (point-in-time).** Restaurant: typical and recent prep time (last 30/60 min), current queue of orders, cuisine, size. Geography: straight and route distance, zone, building type. Traffic: current speed index, congestion. Weather now and short forecast. Supply: couriers available within 2 km and their current load. Time: hour, weekday, holiday, local event. Order: items, size. Recent actual delivery times in the zone (rolling, built with a point-in-time join).

**Label problems.** Orders cancelled or reassigned (censored or noisy); wrong timestamps from the app (clock errors); outliers such as customer not at home. Define rules and clean them. Delivery time includes courier wait, which depends on supply, so ETA and dispatch influence each other.

**Capacity data.** Orders per zone-hour, courier logins and productivity, promotions, weather, school and holiday calendars, new restaurant launches, marketing plans.
model_answer.model:
**ETA baselines.** Per-restaurant median time; a rule: prep time + distance / average speed. These set the bar and are the fallback.

**Main ETA model.** **Gradient-boosted trees** on the features above with a **quantile objective** for several levels (for example 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9), or a median model plus a model for the spread. Optionally predict components (prep, wait, travel) separately and add them: it is easier to debug and to use real-time updates. Deep sequence models on route data can come later for travel time. Update the ETA during the trip, when the courier position and the actual pickup time are known.

**Calibration.** After training, check coverage by segment and apply a simple recalibration (conformal-style adjustment per city and hour block) so that the 80% quantile has about 80% coverage.

**Capacity model.** A global gradient-boosting model or hierarchical model for **orders per zone-hour** with calendar, weather forecast, promotions and lagged volumes, trained with quantile loss. Transform to courier demand with productivity per hour (orders per courier-hour, estimated by city and hour, lower in rain). Planned supply = demand quantile ÷ productivity. For hiring (3-week lead time) use weekly city-level forecasts with trend and seasonality and a wider interval.
model_answer.eval:
**ETA offline.** Time-based split: train on weeks 1-8, validate on weeks 9-10, test on a later week. Metrics: **MAE**, **P90 absolute error**, **bias** (signed), **coverage** of each quantile, and the share of orders finishing inside the promised window. Break down by city, hour, restaurant size, distance, weather, and for new restaurants.

**Baseline comparison.** Report FVA against the fixed-ETA baseline and the simple distance/speed rule.

**Online.** A/B test by city or by randomised customer groups: primary metrics late-rate (more than 10 minutes late), conversion at checkout, support contacts; guardrails: courier earnings and order volume. Watch for interference: dispatch decisions and supply are shared across users in a zone, so randomise by zone-time block (switch-back test).

**Capacity.** Rolling-origin backtest at the lead times that matter (1, 2, 4, 8 weeks), measuring WAPE, bias and **pinball loss** at the planning quantile. Business replay: given the forecast, how many peak hours would have been under-staffed, and how many courier-hours idle? Compare to the current manual plan.
model_answer.serve:
**ETA online path.** At checkout: about 1.2M orders/day, with peak maybe 3x the average: average 14 orders/s, peak about 60-100 orders/s, but ETA is also computed when users **browse restaurants** (maybe 20-50 views per order), so up to **several thousand ETA calls per second** at peak. Latency budget about 50-100 ms. Use a compact tree model in a low-latency service, features from an **online feature store** (rolling restaurant prep times, zone supply, traffic) refreshed every 1-5 minutes, and cache ETA per (restaurant, zone, 5-minute bucket) for browsing; compute the exact value at checkout.

**Fallbacks.** If the feature store is stale or down: use the last cached value or the baseline rule. Sanity bounds (for example ETA between 10 and 120 minutes).

**Training.** Daily or weekly retrain, offline features from the same definitions (no training-serving skew). Challenger model in shadow mode before release.

**Capacity batch.** Nightly job produces zone-hour quantile forecasts for the next 4 weeks, written by upsert with model version and forecast origin. Planners and the scheduling system read the table. About 40 cities × 50 zones × 24 hours × 28 days = 1.3M rows per run: small.
model_answer.monitor:
**Metrics.** ETA: live MAE, P90 error, bias and coverage per city and hour, on-time rate, compared with the baseline; drift (PSI) on key features such as prep time and travel speed; label delay is short (minutes). Capacity: WAPE and tracking signal on orders per zone-hour, and unfilled-peak-hours.

**Failure modes.** Heavy rain or snow: travel time and prep time jump together; add weather features and a fast-reacting rolling feature, and widen the window. Big events (stadium), outage of the restaurant tablet (prep times are unknown), GPS errors, holiday volume spikes, a new city with no history (use global model plus city-level features and a conservative quantile). Concept drift when couriers are added or incentives change (travel waiting time changes).

**Feedback loops.** A longer ETA lowers conversion, which reduces volume, which improves delivery times: the system looks fine. Courier incentives change supply. Restaurants may inflate prep times if they learn that ETA depends on them (gaming). Track these with experiments and with restaurant-level audits.

**Retraining and alerts.** Weekly retrain, extra retrain when coverage of P80 drifts outside 75-85% for a city for 3 days. Alerts have owners and runbooks (fall back to baseline ETA, widen the window).

**Product fairness.** Check that errors are not much worse in particular neighbourhoods.

rubric.item: Separates the two decisions (customer ETA vs weekly capacity) and their horizons
Uses asymmetric costs to choose a promised quantile or window, not just the mean
Lists realistic point-in-time features and defines the label carefully
Proposes baselines and a quantile GBM, with calibration and coverage checks
Plans capacity from a peak/upper-quantile forecast with productivity and lead time (3 weeks)
Evaluates with MAE, P90, bias, coverage, on-time rate by segment and with A/B or switch-back tests
Sizes serving load and latency, uses online features, caching and fallbacks
Monitors drift and coverage, and names failure modes such as weather and outages
Discusses feedback loops (conversion, incentives, restaurant gaming)

follow_ups: Heavy rain starts in one city at 18:00. What does your system do in the first 30 minutes?
How do you provide an ETA for a brand-new restaurant or a brand-new city?
Marketing plans a big discount day. How does your capacity forecast take it into account?
Your P80 ETA has 71% coverage in one city only. How do you debug it?
Customers see a window '25-35 min'. Product wants '25-30 min'. What trade-off do you explain?
How would you use the ETA model inside dispatch (assigning couriers), and what new risks appear?
